Operating system.d: The software that runs a computer: it starts programs, stores files, talks to hardware and keeps users apart. macOS, Windows and Linux are operating systems.

Kernel.d: The core of an operating system that manages the processor, memory, files and hardware. Other programs ask the kernel to do these things for them.

GUI.d: Graphical user interface: using a computer through windows, icons, menus and a mouse, as opposed to typing commands.

Command prompt.d: The short text a shell prints (for example ending in % or $) to show it is ready for your next command. Also the name of Windows' older shell, cmd.exe.

Command.d: A line typed into a shell: a program name, usually followed by options that change how it works and arguments that say what to work on.

zsh.d: The Z shell, the default shell on macOS since macOS 10.15 Catalina. Very similar to bash for everyday commands.

bash.d: The Bourne Again Shell, the most common shell on Linux, in CI pipelines and in shell scripts.

PowerShell.d: Microsoft's shell for Windows (also available on macOS and Linux). Its commands are named Verb-Noun, such as Get-ChildItem.

File.d: A named piece of stored data, such as a document, image, script or log, kept in a folder on disk.

Directory.d: Another word for a folder: a container for files and other directories.

Filesystem.d: The way an operating system organises files and folders on a disk, as a tree of folders starting from a root.

Root directory.d: The top folder of the filesystem tree, written / on macOS and Linux. Every absolute path starts there. On Windows each drive has its own root, such as C:\.

Home directory.d: Your personal folder: /Users/name on macOS, /home/name on Linux, C:\Users\name on Windows. The shell shorthand for it is ~.

Absolute path.d: A file or folder address written in full from the root (starting with / or ~), so it means the same thing wherever you are.

Relative path.d: A file or folder address written from the current working directory, such as tests/login.spec.ts or ../reports. Its meaning depends on where you are.

Hidden file.d: On macOS and Linux, a file or folder whose name starts with a dot, such as .env or .gitignore. Normal listings skip it; it is not protected.

File extension.d: The ending of a file name after the last dot, such as .json or .csv, that labels what kind of content to expect. It is a convention, not a guarantee.

Argument.d: The part of a command that says what to work on, usually a file or folder name, such as notes.txt in cat notes.txt.
